policies.background: Statutory directives under China's 15th Five-Year Plan framework and national climate strategies in order to guarantee the 2030 carbon peaking target, accomplish Nationally Determined Contributions (NDCs), and strengthen China's leadership in global climate governance.

policies.name: 15th Five-Year Plan for Economic and Social Development of the People's Republic of China
policies.background: Responds to the profound and complex changes in the international landscape alongside interwoven structural and cyclical domestic imbalances during the conclusion of the 14th Five-Year Plan in order to lay a solid foundation for achieving Chinese-style modernization and the nation's 2035 economic, technological, and strategic developmental goals.
policies.statusText: Guides China's development priorities in the 2026-2030 period.
policies.keyImplication: This national blueprint creates incentives by opening strategic market scenarios in emerging sectors, driving state capital and patient financing into 'hard tech' innovations, and establishing enhanced tax deductions for corporate R&D. Conversely, it enforces restrictions by subjecting high-risk AI models and algorithms to mandatory security assessments, implementing strict energy and carbon-accounting boundaries across traditional supply chains, and banning non-compliant market-splitting actions via anti-monopoly local protectionism rules.

policies.name: 15th Five-Year Plan for Modernising the National Emergency Management System (State Council No. 15 of 2026)
policies.background: Responds to the strategic requirement of aligning public safety and disaster mitigation with China's 15th Five-Year Plan in order to establish a proactive, modernised, and intelligence-driven national emergency management system focused on risk prevention and disaster resilience by 2035.
policies.statusText: Published on 20 May 2026, implementation in progress.
policies.keyImplication: It imposes regulatory compliance restrictions by mandating all-chain safety inspections, dynamic "ban/restrict/control" negative lists, and strict administrative enforcement ("double-penalty" fines and criminal prosecution) across high-risk sectors such as chemicals, mining, and ultra-high-rise construction. Conversely, it establishes economic incentives for compliant businesses, offering government financing guarantees, preferential funding, fast-track adoption for "first-set" major technical equipment, and rewards for internal hazard reporting.

policies.background: Responds to the strategic mandate of accelerating comprehensive green economic transition and achieving reliable fossil-fuel substitution during the 15th Five-Year Plan period in order to scale up renewable energy supply, enhance grid integration quality, and fulfill China's 2030 carbon peaking commitments.
policies.statusText: Published on 6 July 2026, implementation in progress
policies.keyImplication: It imposes regulatory restrictions by establishing mandatory minimum renewable energy consumption quotas across major energy-consuming industries and enforcing strict grid-connection technical standards (including a minimum 10% firm capacity requirement for new wind and solar farms). Conversely, it creates substantial economic incentives by fast-tracking administrative permitting for integrated multi-energy and microgrid projects, expanding green-certificate trading revenue streams, and implementing capacity payment mechanisms for energy storage and grid-flexibility providers.

policies.name: Announcement on the EU Foreign Subsidies Investigation Constituting Improper Extraterritorial Jurisdiction (Ministry of Justice Notice No. 5 of 2026)
policies.background: Responds to the European Union utilising its Foreign Subsidies Regulation to conduct cross-border data and asset investigations into Nuctech (同方威视) in order to legally block foreign unilateral data gathering and safeguard the commercial information security of Chinese corporate entities from discriminatory economic protectionism.
policies.statusText: Effective from 15 May 2026.
policies.keyImplication: This is the first case covered by the Regulations on Countermeasures against Foreign States' Unlawful Extraterritorial Jurisdiction. This announcement imposes an absolute restriction by completely banning any domestic organisation or individual from executing or assisting with the European Union's cross-border investigation under the Foreign Subsidies Regulation (FSR). It offers zero commercial or regulatory incentives, placing multinational companies under immediate legal jeopardy if they attempt to comply with EU information disclosure requests while operating within China.

regulatoryFramings.label: Corporate legal defense practices, auditing firms, and compliance consultancies

policies.background: The proposal is part of the Tech Sovereignty Package, as well as the AI Continent Action Plan,  and it responds to the 2024 Draghi report and subsequent European Parliament and Council assessments. policies.name: Commission Recommendation on Outbound Investment Screening
policies.background: Building on the 2024 White Paper and public consultations under the European Economic Security Strategy, Commission Recommendation (EU) 2025/63 formally initiates a 15-month fact-finding and data-gathering exercise, directing Member States to monitor and assess risks of technology leakage to third countries from outbound corporate investments in advanced semiconductors, artificial intelligence, and quantum technologies.
policies.statusText: Member States are submitting their final national transaction reports and risk assessments to the Commission, laying the data groundwork for an EU-wide policy proposal expected by late 2026.
policies.keyImplication: The framework establishes a retroactive data-gathering and risk-assessment obligation for corporate entities, requiring the tracking of outbound transactions—including venture capital, joint ventures, and intellectual property transfers—dating back to January 2021 within the semiconductor, artificial intelligence, and quantum technology sectors.

policies.name: Council Recommendation on Enhancing Research Security
policies.background: As a core element of the European Economic Security Strategy, the Recommendation establishes a coordinated EU framework to protect international academic cooperation against foreign interference and unwanted knowledge transfer by integrating security-vetting and risk-management protocols into national research funding mechanisms.
policies.statusText: Passed in May 2024, the framework is midway through its 2025–2027 ERA Policy Agenda timeline; following the rollouts of mandatory research security self-assessment pilots by national funding bodies in early 2026, the Commission is launching a centralized European Centre of Expertise and a digital due diligence screening platform by late 2026.
policies.keyImplication: The framework systematically targets asymmetric technology transfers and 'civil-military fusion' risks involving the EU's competitors, effectively subjecting joint academic partnerships, dual-use deep-tech laboratories, and foreign research personnel to heightened, mandatory national security vetting and grant-eligibility restrictions.

policies.name: Critical Entities Resilience Directive
policies.background: Updating the 2008 European Critical Infrastructure framework, the Critical Entities Resilience Directive shifts the EU legal regime from protecting isolated physical assets to reinforcing systemic, cross-sectoral operational resilience for entities delivering essential societal and economic services against complex hybrid, cyber, climate, and terrorism threats.
policies.statusText: Entering into force on 16 January 2023, the CER Directive set a mandatory Member State national transposition deadline of 17 October 2024 (repealing Directive 2008/114/EC on 18 October 2024), leading into the formal national designation of critical entities by 17 July 2026, with initial Commission compliance and review reports scheduled for July 2027 and June 2029 respectively.
policies.keyImplication: By establishing a standardised non-exhaustive list of essential services across eleven critical sectors, the European Commission provides the mandatory baseline for Member States to conduct risk assessments and officially designate their national critical entities by 17 July 2026, triggering enforceable operational resilience and risk-mitigation obligations for designated operators.

policies.name: Critical Raw Materials Act
policies.background: Responds to the 2022 Versailles Declaration and growing supply security risks by embedding raw material resilience into the Green Deal Industrial Plan to accelerate internal net-zero technology manufacturing and end strategic dependencies on concentrated foreign imports.
policies.statusText: The initial 2024 regulation is fully active, while a package of targeted 2025 amendments—expanding permanent magnet recycling parameters and shift-assigning corporate supply-chain audit oversight to the Commission—is currently under active interinstitutional negotiation following the Council’s March 2026 position and the Parliament's April 2026 review.
policies.keyImplication: Establishes specific 2030 quantitative benchmarks (10% extraction, 40% processing, 25% recycling, 65% single-country import cap) exclusively for Strategic Raw Materials, while regulating broader Critical Raw Materials through non-binding Commission consumption projections and qualitative national circularity/efficiency frameworks. Fast-tracks 'Strategic Project' permits and mandates supply chain audits for large tech and defense firms.

policies.name: Cyber Resilience Act
policies.background: Building on the 2020 EU Cybersecurity Strategy and complementing existing legal frameworks like the NIS2 Directive, the Cyber Resilience Act establishes unified EU-wide security standards for digital products to mitigate massive economic losses from data breaches and secure critical supply chains against escalating cyber threats.
policies.statusText: While full application of the Cyber Resilience Act begins on 11 December 2027, its enforcement follows a phased rollout starting with conformity assessment body provisions on 11 June 2026, followed on 11 September 2026 by mandatory incident reporting requiring manufacturers to submit an early warning within 24 hours of detecting actively exploited vulnerabilities or severe incidents, a full notification within 72 hours, and a final report within 14 days of a mitigation or 1 month of an incident.
policies.keyImplication: The regulation establishes mandatory CE-marking compliance, lifetime vulnerability management, and 24-hour incident reporting across digital supply chains, compelling vendors to disclose full Software Bills of Materials (SBOM) and undergo third-party auditing via EU importers or designated bodies.

policies.name: Elements for a New EU Strategy on China
policies.background: Replacing a decade-old strategic baseline to adapt to economic and political developments involving China, this Joint Communication established an updated policy framework for EU engagement centered on reciprocal market access, level-playing-field economic competition, principled defense of human rights and international law, and reinforced internal EU unity across Member State bilateral relations.
policies.statusText: Adopted on 22 June 2016; endorsed by Council Conclusions on 18 July 2016; succeeded and reframed by the 2019 EU-China – A Strategic Outlook.
policies.keyImplication: The Joint Communication shifted the EU’s baseline to an interest-driven policy focusing on economic reciprocity, level-playing-field conditions, and Member State cohesion. It preceded the EU's defensive trade and economic security architecture.

policies.name: EU Industrial Maritime Strategy
policies.background: This strategy responds to Europe's loss of global market share to state-subsidised foreign shipbuilders and growing hybrid security threats to underwater and port infrastructure, establishing an industrial roadmap to strengthen the resilience of waterborne supply chains.
policies.statusText: The Council approved conclusions on 8 June 2026.
policies.keyImplication: The strategy transitions Europe into an active defender of its own domestic naval industrial base, deploying an EU Industrial Maritime Value Chains Alliance, strict non-price procurement criteria to favor European shipyards, and dedicated funding to ramp up dual-use and naval production capacity.

policies.name: EU Ports Strategy
policies.background: This strategy responds to growing foreign state-backed ownership control over critical European maritime infrastructure, escalating cyber and hybrid threats, and the infiltration of organised crime networks, establishing a security and investment framework to strengthen sovereign control over the single market's primary logistical trade gateways.
policies.statusText: Adopted. Member states approved the Council conclusions on 8 June 2026.
policies.keyImplication: The strategy transforms EU port policy from open asset monetisation to strict defensive security management, introducing harmonized background-check frameworks for port workers, formal guidance restricting high-risk foreign direct investment, and mandatory port-centred energy grids designed to accelerate alternative fuel bunkering and military mobility transit.

policies.name: EU Steel Regulation
policies.background: It addresses global overcapacity and trade diversion by setting an annual 18.3-million-tonne duty-free quota with a 50% out-of-quota tariff across 26 steel product categories. Except for European Economic Area (EEA) partners, the measure applies universally and introduces a strict 'melt and pour' origin requirement to ensure supply chain transparency and prevent circumvention.
policies.statusText: Applies from 1 July 2026.
policies.keyImplication: Tightens market access for foreign steel exporters while closing transshipment loopholes through third countries via origin tracking. For downstream EU industries, it shifts procurement toward domestic or verified Free Trade Area (FTA) supply chains, providing capital protection for European steelmakers investing in decarbonisation.

policies.statusText: Entering into force on 16 January 2023, the NIS2 Directive required Member States to transpose rules by 17 October 2024 (repealing Directive (EU) 2016/1148 on 18 October 2024), while a newly proposed 2026 targeted amendment package, currently undergoing ordinary legislative procedure, aims to streamline compliance through post-quantum cryptography mandates, European Union Agency for Cybersecurity (ENISA) cross-border supervision, and organisational certification schemes ahead of the initial triennial Commission review due by 17 October 2027.

policies.name: The Cybersecurity Act 2
policies.background: Responds to a significantly worsening cyber threat landscape and sophisticated state-sponsored hybrid attacks in order to reinforce Europe's digital sovereignty, secure critical ICT supply chains against foreign interference, and streamline compliance across the Union.
policies.statusText: Under legislative debate (first reading). The public feedback window closed on 12 May 2026. The file was assigned to the Committee on Industry, Research and Energy (ITRE) with Markéta Gregorová (Greens/EFA, CZ) serving as the appointed rapporteur. The file is currently under committee review in the European Parliament, balanced by formal advisory input from EU consultative bodies.
policies.keyImplication: Mandates the exclusion and de-risking of high-risk third-country ICT suppliers from European mobile telecommunications networks and 18 critical infrastructure sectors to prevent foreign interference and strategic dependencies; for compliant businesses, it introduces incentives such as an enhanced, voluntary European Cybersecurity Certification Framework (ECCF) that simplifies compliance with EU rules.

policies.name: The EU Strategy for Cooperation in the Indo-Pacific
policies.background: Adopted in September 2021 and updated via formal Council Conclusions in October 2025, this strategy was triggered by the EU's growing vulnerability to maritime chokepoint disruptions and critical supply chain vulnerabilities in the Indo-Pacific, and it aims to establish a comprehensive geopolitical framework to secure diversified economic networks and defend freedom of navigation.
policies.statusText: Launched in September 2021. The Council of the European Union approved conclusions on the implementation of the strategy on 20 October 2025.
policies.keyImplication: The strategy shifts Europe’s external posture from mostly commercial diplomacy to a multi-layered presence in the Indo-Pacific, leveraging an expanded network of trade agreements, sovereign digital partnerships, and coordinated naval deployments to secure critical maritime sea lanes and build diversified, high-resilience supply networks capable of withstanding geopolitical turbulence.

policies.background: Responds to demographic aging, chronic disease expansion, and structural healthcare resource disparities in order to establish a high-quality, digitalised, and integrated health service system while deepening health-medicare-pharmaceutical governance under the Healthy China 2030 framework.

policies.name: White Paper on Export Controls
policies.background: Released as part of the 2024 Economic Security Package, this initiative proposes to modernise the EU's dual-use export control framework by introducing fast-track mechanisms for unilateral EU-wide control lists and establishing cross-notification requirements to better coordinate national security restrictions across Member States.
policies.statusText: Adopted. The core objectives of the White Paper have been structurally operationalized via the European Commission's adoption of autonomous Delegated Regulations that complement deadlocked multilateral regimes to unilaterally expand the EU's dual-use control list for advanced technologies.
policies.keyImplication: The framework shifts dual-use technology oversight toward an autonomous EU-level mechanism, enabling rapid harmonisation of export restrictions on emerging technologies independent of deadlocked multilateral regimes.
